Ok, I am asked to explain why I'm not doing exactly why Obsidian is doing. Can you get to the heart of the sub-optimality of copying the Obsidian importedAssets structure (assuming the transfer of assets to firebase as a given)

The short version you can hand someone:

> Obsidian's `importedAssets` is a per-note index over a store Obsidian can enumerate and address by name. Roam has neither property, so copying the structure gives us its costs without its benefits.

Two concrete asymmetries under that.

**1. Scope. The record would be per-page; the thing it describes is per-graph.**

In Obsidian the imported file lands in the note's own neighbourhood, so a per-note record matches the scope of what it tracks. A Roam upload is a **graph-level resource** — one URL, valid from any page, reusable by every node that references the same asset. Splitting a graph-level fact across N per-page records means the question we actually ask on every sync — *"have I already uploaded this hash?"* — can only be answered by reading every imported page.

Obsidian never has to ask that question, because it can ask the vault instead: `getFirstLinkpathDest` resolves a path to a file, and the path is one Obsidian chose. The frontmatter is a convenience over an authoritative, queryable store. Roam's storage isn't queryable at all — its own docs say "there's no way to search for those leftover files yet" — so a per-page record wouldn't be a cache over anything. It would be the only copy, in the wrong shape.

**2. Redundancy — and this is the part that's specific to us.**

Obsidian *cannot* name imported files `imported-<hash>`, because in a vault the filename is load-bearing UI: it's what the user sees, links to, and searches for. So Obsidian has no choice but to carry the hash in a side-table.

Roam's filenames are invisible — we checked, nothing in the UI ever surfaces them. That same uselessness is what frees us to put the identity *in the file itself*. Once we do, the per-page mapping becomes recomputable from the page's own blocks: the URLs are in the content, and each URL's name tells you which asset it is. Persisting it stores a second copy of something already on the page.

**So the two failures compound.** A per-page record would be individually *insufficient* for the graph-level question, and individually *redundant* against the page it's attached to. More state, less answer.

Worth saying explicitly, because it defuses the "Obsidian does it, so why don't you" framing: **Obsidian's structure is correct for Obsidian.** It encodes two assumptions about the host — an enumerable store, and filenames that must stay human-meaningful. Neither holds in Roam. We did copy the pattern at first, and dropped it once we confirmed the hash survives in the filename; the one map we kept is the piece that's genuinely expensive to recompute.
When you speak of enumeration, it makes sense to me because I have shared context. It does not make sense to others. Can you develop?

Fair — "enumerable" is doing a lot of work there. Here's the same point without the shorthand.

## What Roam's storage actually offers

Roam's file API has exactly three operations:

```
  upload(file)  -> gives you back a URL
  get(url)      -> gives you back the file
  delete(url)   -> removes it
```

Every one of them requires a URL you already hold. There is **no "list the files in this graph"** and no "is there a file for X." Roam's own documentation says as much: *"There's no way to search for those leftover files yet."*

So a file whose URL you've lost is, from your code's point of view, gone — while still sitting in storage consuming quota. You can't find it, count it, or check whether it exists.

## The question both systems have to answer

*"I'm about to import this image. Do I already have a copy?"*

**Obsidian can look it up.** It knows where it would have put the file, because *it* chose the path. So it asks the vault directly: is there a file there? The vault answers. The `importedAssets` record in frontmatter is a shortcut over that — delete the frontmatter and Obsidian can still find the file by looking in the folder.

**Roam can only remember.** It didn't choose the URL; Roam generated a random one at upload time. There's no location to check and no way to search. If we didn't write the URL down, there is no second way to recover it.

Put simply: **Obsidian can look, Roam can only remember.**

## The analogy, if it helps

Obsidian's vault is a filing cabinet. You can open it, flip through, and see what's in there.

Roam's storage is a left-luggage counter that only accepts a ticket. Hand over the ticket, you get your bag. Lose the ticket and the bag is still on the rack — permanently — but nobody, including the counter staff, can tell you which one is yours or even that it's there. There's no walking the racks.

Obsidian's per-note record is like jotting down which coat you checked: handy, but if you lose the note you can still go look in your own closet. In Roam there's no closet to look in. The note *is* the only access.

## Why that changes the shape, not just the reliability

Because Obsidian can look, its record is a convenience and its shape barely matters — per-note is fine, since the vault backstops it.

Because Roam can't look, whatever we write down is the only access we have. That makes the shape the whole decision: it has to answer the question we actually ask, which is graph-wide (*"anywhere in this graph, do I have this asset?"*). A per-page record can't answer a graph-wide question without reading every page — so copying Obsidian's shape would leave us with the only copy of the data, in a form that can't answer the only question we ask of it.

Ok. It's stupid but I'm asked to hew closer to Obsidian, and so we'll store the importedAssets in the page. This will solve the problem of duplicates while re-syncing the same page, but not that of graph-wide duplicate, which I'm asked to ignore.

Understood — proceeding on that basis.

The good news for the "hew closer" goal: it lands on *literally* Obsidian's structure, with one substitution.

```
  obsidian:   frontmatter.importedAssets  { "<sha256>": "<vault path>" }
  roam:       page props .importedAssets  { "<sha256>": "<firebase url>" }
```

Same shape, same scope, same lookup. Easier to defend as a parallel than what we had.

**One sub-decision it forces:** on re-sync, do you prune entries whose assets the new content no longer references, or accumulate?

I'd **accumulate** — it matches Obsidian, which adds to `fm.importedAssets` and never prunes, and it means an image removed and later restored doesn't trigger a fresh upload. The cost is a page prop that grows monotonically, which is small. Pruning would keep it tidy at the price of re-uploading on any remove-then-restore.

**What it costs, stated once so it's on the record:** the same asset referenced from two imported nodes uploads twice, and a page deleted and re-imported uploads again. Those duplicates are permanent, since nothing collects them.

**What it actually buys, which isn't nothing:**

- **No well-known registry page to bootstrap.** That was a real wart — where does it live, what if the user deletes or renames it, how do you find it again. Per-page props need none of that.
- **One fewer sign-off item.** "If someone deletes the registry page, reuse restarts from scratch" disappears; there's no such page. The acceptance ask reduces to just the deliberate orphans.
- **Deleting a page now cleanly discards its own record**, which is consistent with the uploads becoming orphans — a state we already tolerate.

**What's unchanged, and now matters more:** the `imported-<sha256>` filename. With per-page maps there's no graph-wide view anywhere in our data, so the files themselves become the only route to one. If anyone ever wants a cleanup pass or a cross-page dedup, that name is what makes it possible. I'd hold onto it firmly.

Everything else stands: no schema change, no GC tracking, media-type-aware link rewriting with filename labels, explicit size cap.

Want me to update `design.md` and the four docs? Decision 4 gets rewritten around the per-page map, the Obsidian-comparison block in Decision 3 gets simpler (the structure *does* transfer now), and the sign-off shrinks to one item. Tell me prune or accumulate and I'll fold that in at the same time.
Agree with accumulate. I think we can proceed accordingly. Also assume the filename is baked in.

5. Write the map back.

**Entries accumulate; they are never pruned.** An asset the new content no longer references keeps its entry, matching Obsidian, which adds to `fm.importedAssets` and never removes. The benefit is that an asset removed and later restored does not trigger a fresh upload; the cost is a page property that grows monotonically, which is small.

*Why a map at all:* `file.upload` is not idempotent, and re-sync rebuilds a page's content from scratch. Without a record, every re-sync re-uploads every asset on the page. Note this is about *not creating* garbage, which is a separate concern from collecting it (Decision 6).

*Why the key is the content hash:* Supabase stores one blob per unique file, referenced from many notes under different `filepath`s, so the hash identifies the bytes and the source filename does not.

**Deduplication is per page, not per graph — accepted.**

The same asset referenced from two imported nodes uploads twice, and a page deleted and re-imported uploads again. Those duplicates are permanent, since nothing collects them (Decision 6).

This is a deliberate choice to stay close to Obsidian's structure rather than the narrowly optimal one. A graph-level map would answer the graph-wide question — *anywhere in this graph, do I already hold this asset?* — which a per-page map cannot answer without reading every page. The trade was made knowingly, and it is not free, but it buys two things: there is no well-known registry page to bootstrap, locate, or repair if a user renames or deletes it, and deleting a page cleanly discards its own record, leaving orphaned uploads in a state the design already tolerates.

**Name every upload `imported-<sha256>.<ext>`.**

Verified end to end: uploading a `File` named `imported-deadbeef.txt` and calling `file.get` on the returned URL yields `name: imported-deadbeef.txt`, and the name is separately readable from `metadata["file-name"]` without downloading the bytes (see Context).

This matters more under a per-page map than it would under a graph-level one, because **no graph-wide view of mirrored assets exists anywhere in our data**. The files themselves are the only route to one. Anything that later wants to deduplicate across pages, audit what a graph holds, or drive a cleanup has to start by reading names off the URLs present in imported pages. Treat the convention as load-bearing rather than cosmetic.

**Label non-image links with the source filename.**

`file.upload` returns a bare URL for anything that is not an image, PDF, audio or video, and a bare URL in a Roam block renders as a link whose visible text *is* the URL — a hundred-odd characters of storage uid that tells the reader nothing. The rewriting step must therefore emit `[report.docx](url)`, taking the label from the source markdown's display text or the basename of its path, rather than dropping the returned URL in raw. The name is otherwise never surfaced anywhere in Roam: images render as images, media types render in a viewer, and `metadata["file-name"]` is read by nothing in the Roam UI. This link label is the only place a user ever sees what an imported file is called. (The bare-URL rendering is inferred from the reference, not observed — confirm against a real graph.)

*Alternatives considered:*
- **A graph-level `assetRegistry` keyed by hash.** Narrowly better — it deduplicates across the whole graph, which is the question the sync actually asks. Set aside in favour of matching Obsidian's structure; see the accepted trade above. If graph-wide duplication later proves costly, this is the change to make, and the filename convention is what makes a migration to it possible.
- **A Supabase table keyed `(grantee_space_id, filehash)`.** Rejected: server state for what is client-side graph bookkeeping, and graph props keep working if the user stops using our backend.

'''
lines[start:end] = new.split("\n")
p.write_text("\n".join(lines))
print("decision 4 rewritten")

content.text:
All six files updated and consistent; HTML validates clean on both.

**The structure is now literally Obsidian's**, which makes the parallel easy to point at:

```
  obsidian:  frontmatter.importedAssets   { "<sha256>": "<vault path>" }
  roam:      page props .importedAssets   { "<sha256>": "<firebase url>" }
```

Accumulate, never prune — matching Obsidian, and noted as such so it doesn't read as an oversight later.

Three consequences I made explicit rather than leaving implied:

- **Decision 3's Obsidian comparison flipped.** It used to explain why the bookkeeping *doesn't* transfer. It now says the bookkeeping is the one part that does, and only the vault-dependent half doesn't. That block exists to answer "why aren't you doing what Obsidian does," so it had to change direction.
- **The registry-loss risk is gone; a duplication risk replaced it.** There's no registry page to lose. In its place: per-page dedup means the cost scales with how often labs reuse a figure across shared nodes — which I flagged as unmeasured, since neither of us knows that number.
- **The sign-off dropped to two items** in the triage doc and two in the brief. "If the map is lost, reuse restarts" disappeared entirely; the per-page duplication took its slot, since that's now the thing being accepted rather than a mechanism detail.

The filename convention is written up as **load-bearing rather than cosmetic** in both `design.md` and the brief. That's the one place I leaned harder than before: with per-page maps there's no graph-wide view of mirrored assets anywhere in our data, so `imported-<sha256>` is the only handle anything future could use — a cross-page dedup pass, an audit, or a migration to the graph-level map if duplication ever proves costly. Worth defending if anyone proposes simplifying it away.

The graph-level map is recorded as a rejected alternative with its rationale intact, so the option is documented rather than erased.
Note: You still have Obsidian's solution in the rejected alternatives of option 3 in design.md, at line 72

result.output: 64 ### 3. Mirror Obsidian-origin assets to Firebase, choosing durability over revocability 65 66 At import time the Roam client downloads the asset from the Supabase bucket with its authenticated client and re-uploads it via `file.upload`, then rewrites the markdown link to the returned URL. 67 68 *Why:* Roam renders `![](url)` as an ``, which issues an **anonymous cross-origin GET** — no `Authorization` header, and cookies are third-party. Whatever the destination markdown points at must be fetchable with no credentials. Supabase-hosted bytes have no such URL. 69 70 *Alternatives considered:* 71 72 - **Do what Obsidian's importer already does** — download the asset and keep a local copy, linking to it by path. This is the obvious precedent and the question gets asked every time, so it is worth answering explicitly: Obsidian's strategy works because Obsidian has a filesystem, and each half of it depends on that. 73 - *Nowhere to put the bytes.* Obsidian writes the asset into the vault and links to it by path. A Roam page can only point at a URL; there is no local copy to make. 74 - *The fetch is not ours to make.* Obsidian's plugin downloads with an authenticated Supabase client. In Roam the fetch is performed by the browser's `` tag, anonymously — no auth header, no usable cookies — so the private bucket is unreachable from there and the file has to end up somewhere public. 75 - *We do not choose the location.* Obsidian picks the vault path, so it is stable and re-import is idempotent for free: the filesystem **is** the registry, resolved by `getFirstLinkpathDest`. Roam's `file.upload` assigns a fresh random URL on every call, so what the filesystem guarantees Obsidian for nothing, Roam has to be told. 76 - The part that *does* transfer is Obsidian's stored bookkeeping: `frontmatter.importedAssets` maps hash to vault path, and Decision 4 keeps the same per-note map with the URL substituted for the path. What cannot transfer is everything above, which depends on the vault being somewhere Obsidian can write to and look in. 77 78 - **Serve from a Vercel route** at `/api/assets/`, backed by the private bucket, following the existing `apps/website/app/api/supabase/**` pattern. This is a genuinely strong design and the main casualty of this decision. It is better on almost every axis: no duplicate blobs, one URL per asset per graph, no consumption of the user's Roam storage quota, and — the real prize — **revocable**, at two levels. It needs a small `AssetGrant(token, grantee_space_id, filehash)` table with `UNIQUE (grantee_space_id, filehash)`, and one new space-anchored SQL helper, because as noted in Context every existing access function bottoms out in `auth.uid()` and cannot be evaluated for an anonymous `` request. 79 80 Rejected for v0 on a single trade: **irrevocable is the same property as durable.** The Vercel route makes every imported image in every Roam graph depend on a service we operate; if it stops, the images stop. Firebase-mirrored copies keep rendering if our backend goes away, the org stops paying, or the project winds down. For lab notes meant to outlive the tooling, that is the more valuable property, and the team's earlier acceptance of public Firebase URLs points the same way. 81 82 Note also what the route does *not* buy: it is not privacy. A capability URL in a Roam page is a bearer token in plaintext, readable by anyone who can read the page. It converts "public forever" into "public until revoked," which is a real gain but a narrower one than it first appears. 83 84 - **Signed Supabase URLs.** Rejected: they expire, and the URL is persisted into page content that outlives any expiry. 85 86 - **A Roam-side `FileReference` row**, so the mirrored URL has a home in the database. Rejected because it is blocked twice over: `file_reference_update_policy` requires `in_space(space_id, 'editor')` and the importing user is not an editor of the source Obsidian space; and the FK to `Content` would require fabricating a `Document` + `Content` + `PlatformAccount` triple for a node that was never published. content.text:
Fixed. The Obsidian comparison is now its own sub-section of Decision 3 — **"What transfers from Obsidian's importer, and what does not"** — sitting above the alternatives rather than inside them. It splits explicitly:

- *The storage half does not transfer* — the three filesystem-dependent reasons, unchanged.
- *The bookkeeping half does transfer* — `frontmatter.importedAssets` → the per-page map, same shape, same scope, same lookup.

`Alternatives considered` now contains only things actually rejected: the Vercel route, signed URLs, and the Roam-side `FileReference` row.

That also makes the document read correctly for the question you keep getting asked. A reader who lands on Decision 3 to find out why we're not doing what Obsidian does now gets "we are, for the part that can transfer" as a first-class answer, rather than finding Obsidian's approach filed under rejected with a correction buried in the last sub-bullet.
Do we need the triage file now? How are we exceeding the linear task scopes?

Two answers, and the second turns up something that needs a ticket edit, not just a re-cut.

## The triage file has outlived its purpose

It was worth writing when the framing was "should this become work." But the tickets predate it — ENG-1864 and four follow-ups are already scoped, in a milestone, on a project. The outcome was never in doubt, and its one piece of unique content is the re-cut recommendation.

Everything else in it now duplicates the brief: same problem statement, same acceptance items, same shape. I'd **drop both triage files** and put the re-cut recommendation where it acts — as a comment on ENG-1872. Unless your process requires a triage record before ticket surgery, in which case keep the markdown and delete the HTML.

## Scope drift, in both directions

| ticket | as written | as designed | |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1864** contract | metadata incl. MIME, size, access scope | types + fixtures + behaviour matrix; no `accessScope`, no stored MIME/size | **narrower** |
| **1870** publish Roam refs | detect **and persist** references | detect and report; persists nothing | **narrower — see below** |
| **1871** validate Obsidian output | inspect, validate, log gaps | unchanged | matches |
| **1872** import into Roam | consume metadata, preserve links, report | upload pipeline, per-page map, filename convention, media-type rewriting, size cap | **much wider** |
| **1873** validate Obsidian import | run helpers against Roam-origin fixtures | already passes; near no-op | **narrower** |

**The one that actually breaks: ENG-1870.** Its Done When says *"Available asset bytes or stable URL-only references are persisted with the node's access scope."* We decided to persist nothing (Decision 1 — no consumer) and to drop access scope entirely (Decision 7). That criterion cannot be met as written, so the ticket needs its description edited, not just resequenced. Left alone, whoever picks it up either builds write-only rows or fails review.

**ENG-1872 is the over-scope one**, as flagged: it describes "consume shared asset metadata where available," and there is no metadata to consume — we parse markdown instead. Its Done When is still satisfiable, but the work behind it is several times what the text implies.

**1864's Done When survives** — it asks for typed payloads and fixtures, both of which we deliver. Access scope and MIME/size appear only in its Solution section, so that's a documented deviation rather than a failed criterion.

**1873 is nearly free** and 1871 holds.

So the ticket work is: rewrite 1870's description, rewrite 1872's and split it, and note the 1864 deviations. Want me to draft those three descriptions here for you to paste, or create the 1872 sub-issues directly? Both write to Linear, so I'll wait for the word either way.
Please write revisions as a roam-style markdown, which I'll get approved before writing to Linear.

    - Proposed title: **Detect and report asset references in Roam-origin shared nodes**
    - Problem
        - Roam shared-node markdown may reference images or files held in Roam's own storage.
        - Those references have to survive into the destination app, and anything unusable should be reported rather than silently dropped.
    - Solution
        - Detect asset references in the `full` markdown of Roam-origin shared nodes.
        - Leave the URLs in place. They are already world-readable, and the destination resolves them by following the link.
        - Report references that cannot be used alongside the publish result.
    - Done When
        - Asset references in Roam-origin shared node markdown are detected and counted.
        - Roam-origin markdown reaches the destination with its asset URLs intact.
        - Unusable references are reported without failing node publication.
    - Out of Scope
        - Persisting asset references to the database. Nothing would read them, and a work list is derivable from `Content.text` at any time.

- **ENG-1872** — needs a rewrite and a split
    - Why: the current description says "consume shared asset metadata where available." There is no metadata to consume — assets are found by parsing markdown. The real work is an upload path plus bookkeeping, several times what the text implies.
    - Proposed title: **Copy Obsidian-origin assets into Roam on import**
    - Problem
        - Obsidian attachments live in a private Supabase bucket, with no URL a browser can fetch without credentials.
        - Roam can only embed a URL, so an imported node's images will not render unless the bytes are copied somewhere Roam can reach.
        - Roam's upload API returns a new URL on every call, and re-sync rebuilds a page from scratch — so without a record, every re-sync duplicates every asset.
    - Solution
        - On materialization, copy each referenced Obsidian asset into Roam's own storage via `roamAlphaAPI.file.upload`.
        - Record hash → URL in an `importedAssets` map on the imported page's properties, mirroring Obsidian's `frontmatter.importedAssets`.
        - Name each upload `imported-<sha256>` so the copy is self-identifying.
        - Rewrite links with Roam's native embed syntax per media type, labelling non-media links with the source filename.
        - Leave external `http(s)` URLs untouched.
    - Done When
        - An Obsidian-origin node with an image imports into Roam and the image renders.
        - Re-syncing the same node does not re-upload assets that page already copied.
        - A node containing a PDF, an audio file and an external URL produces correct Roam syntax for each.
        - An asset that fails to copy leaves its original token in place and comes back in the import result, without failing the node.
    - Out of Scope
        - Deduplication across pages. Per-page only, matching Obsidian's structure; the same asset used by two nodes is copied twice.
        - Deleting or tracking unused copies.
        - Surfacing failures to the user — ENG-1877 owns that.
        - Asset refresh when upstream bytes change.
    - Notes
        - design.md Decisions 3 through 6.
        - Needs an explicit size cap of its own; it cannot inherit Obsidian's publish cap, which is expected to rise.
- **Proposed ENG-1872 sub-issues**
    - **a — Per-page asset map accessor**
        - Read and write `importedAssets` on an imported page's props, under the existing discourse-graph namespace beside `importedFrom`.
        - Entries accumulate and are never pruned, matching Obsidian.
        - Done when: get/set round-trips, unit tested, and documented as a cache that is safe to lose.
        - Depends on nothing. Can start immediately.
    - **b — Copy one asset into Roam storage**
        - Given a hash and bytes: build a `File` named `imported-<sha256>.<ext>`, call `file.upload`, unwrap the media-type-dependent return value to a bare URL, record the entry.
        - Apply an explicit size cap; over-cap returns a skip result rather than throwing.
        - Done when: two copies of the same hash on one page produce one upload, and unwrapping covers all five return shapes — `![](url)`, `{{[[pdf]]: url}}`, `{{[[audio]]: url}}`, `{{[[video]]: url}}`, bare URL.
        - Depends on a.
    - **c — Rewrite asset links in materialized markdown**
        - Find asset tokens in Obsidian-origin markdown, resolve each to a hash, emit Roam-native syntax per media type, label non-image links with the source filename, leave `http(s)` untouched.
        - Done when: the ENG-1864 fixtures round-trip, and a node with an image, a PDF and an external URL each come out correct.
        - Depends on ENG-1864. Independent of a and b — develop against a stub URL resolver.
    - **d — Wire asset copying into materializeSharedNode**
        - New stage between fetch-content and replace-page-content.
        - Asset failures never fail the node: unresolved assets keep their original token and are returned in the result.
        - Done when: a node whose asset 404s still imports with an intact body.
        - Depends on b and c.
    - a and c can run in parallel. b concentrates the fiddly API detail, c the fiddly markdown detail — keeping them apart is most of the value of splitting.
- **ENG-1864** — no rewrite needed, one note to add
    - Its Done When asks for typed payloads and fixtures, both of which the design delivers. The deviations are in its Solution section only.
    - Suggested Notes bullet: "Two items from the original solution were designed out and are documented in design.md: `accessScope` (Decision 7 — read access is already determined by row-level security on the referencing node, so a per-asset field would be a weaker duplicate) and stored MIME/size (Decision 1 — no consumer; both are available from the storage metadata when needed)."

# DG Engineering Writing Style

Write in a direct, concise, plainspoken style that preserves important context and qualification.

## Core style

- Lead with the relevant point and move quickly to the concrete question, request, or action.
- Prefer the shortest version that remains clear and preserves necessary nuance.
- Identify wording or missing context that is ambiguous or could be misconstrued. Resolve it when the intended meaning is clear; otherwise, flag it and ask for clarification.
- Use natural contractions and everyday wording. Avoid corporate jargon, inflated phrasing, and generic professional filler.
- Avoid em dashes as sentence-level punctuation. Use a period, comma, colon, semicolon, or parentheses to separate thoughts instead. Preserve em dashes only when they appear in exact quotations, titles, source text, or technical content supplied by the requester.
- When identifying a problem or disagreement, state it plainly and pivot toward clarification, resolution, criteria, or next steps.
- Prefer bullets for distinct points. When prose reads more naturally, keep paragraphs and sentences short; avoid run-on sentences.
- Ask one clear question when one will do. Combine related questions only when separating them would add needless length.

## Adapt to the channel

- For a quick reply or chat message, omit the greeting and sign-off when they add no value.
- For technical issues, describe the observed behavior, the relevant contrast or expectation, and the requested clarification or next step.
- For engineering tickets and technical documentation, apply these ASD-STE100-inspired principles:
  - Use one term consistently for each concept. Do not alternate between synonyms.
  - Put one primary action or idea in each sentence.
  - Prefer active voice when the actor is important.
  - Replace vague verbs such as "handle," "support," or "improve" with the specific behavior or result.

## Drafting rules

- Preserve facts, commitments, dates, names, links, and technical meaning supplied by the requester.
- Do not invent availability, decisions, commitments, or emotional language.
- Treat explicit directions such as "shorter," "warmer," "more forceful," "broader," or "one sentence" as overrides for the current draft.
- When the requester asks for alternatives, vary the framing or emphasis rather than making superficial synonym swaps.
- Return a ready-to-use draft first. Add explanation only when requested or when an ambiguity materially affects the wording.

# DG Create Engineering Ticket

Create an Engineering ticket that another engineer can understand and implement without rediscovering its intent or scope.

Use `$dg-engineering-writing-style` when available. It is in the repository's `./.agents/skills` folder.

## Canonical template

The canonical Linear template is [General Engineering Task](https://linear.app/discourse-graphs/new?template=6ca39698-3bce-449a-992e-059f0334e15b). Keep this link only as a reference in this skill. Never add it to a created ticket.

Use this exact template as the drafting checklist:

```markdown
## Problem

- What accepted user, developer, or project need does this address?
- Why does it need to be solved now?

## Solution

- What is the smallest change that solves the problem?

## Done When

- Describe how success is verified (behavioral or technical).
- Remember: Make only the smallest change needed to solve the problem.
- Remember: **Stay within the defined scope, or communicate any scope increase**

## Out of Scope

- (Optional) What adjacent cases, abstractions, or future work are explicitly not included?
- Link follow-up tickets where applicable

## Notes

- Additional Context, Blockers, dependencies, or follow-up actions.
```

Every bullet above is placeholder guidance. Replace or remove every placeholder before presenting a draft or creating a ticket. Keep all five headings, leaving `Out of Scope` or `Notes` empty when nothing useful applies. Use 1–3 short bullets per section unless the ticket is genuinely complex.

## Ticket readiness

Always use the Engineering team. This skill never creates or redirects to Feedback.

- Use `Backlog` when the problem is known, the fix is agreed upon, and another engineer can implement it without further product or solution decisions.
- Use `Triage` when implementation is likely within six months but the decision, scope, or solution is not fully settled.
- Keep an explicit Engineering ticket request in Engineering even when it is idea-stage.

## Project selection

Every ticket must use an existing project that is not completed, canceled, archived, or trashed. Resolve the project in this order:

1. Use the project explicitly named by the user.
2. Use a clearly relevant active project from the current work context.
3. For Roam work, use `Roam Discourse Graph plugin assorted tasks`.
4. For Obsidian work, use `Obsidian Discourse Graphs plugin assorted tasks`.
5. Otherwise, use `Engineering Ops assorted tasks`.

Confirm the selected project still exists, is active, and includes the Engineering team. Never create a project. If a user-specified project is missing, ambiguous, or inactive, ask the user for another project instead of silently substituting one.

## Labels and optional fields

- Inspect existing issue labels and apply every clearly relevant label.
- Never create a label or guess an uncertain label.
- Missing or uncertain labels do not block creation. After creation, tell the user when no label was applied or when label selection remained uncertain.
- Set priority only when the user or context makes it clear and useful.
- Do not set a cycle or release. CI/CD handles releases.

## Create or draft

Draft without changing Linear when the user asks for a draft, review, or rewrite. Create the ticket without an additional confirmation when the user explicitly asks to create it.

Before creation, resolve the current Engineering statuses, selected project, and existing labels. Create the issue once with its title, completed description, status, project, labels, and justified priority. If the result is ambiguous, search for the issue before retrying so a transient failure does not create a duplicate.

After creation, return the issue identifier, title, status, project, and link. Include the generated branch name when Linear returns one. Do not restate the full description unless the user asks.

# Linear ticket revisions: cross-app assets

Draft only. Nothing has been written to Linear.

Shared metadata for every ticket below:

- Team: Engineering
- Project: Push and pull nodes between Roam and Obsidian (existing, active)
- Milestone: Relations and assets
- Status: Backlog. The design is settled and needs no further solution decisions.
- Labels: `Roam plugin` on all. `Share and publish` additionally on ENG-1870.

Design reference: `design.md` in the `cross-app-asset-references` OpenSpec change.

---

## ENG-1870 (rewrite)

**Proposed title:** Detect and report asset references in Roam-origin shared nodes

**Why the rewrite:** the current Done When requires persisting each reference with an access scope. Nothing reads a stored reference, and row-level security on the node already determines access. The criterion cannot be met as written.

### Problem

- Roam shared-node markdown can reference images and files held in Roam's storage. Those references must survive publication so a destination app can resolve them.
- A reference that cannot be used should be reported, not dropped silently.

### Solution

- Detect asset references in the `full` markdown of Roam-origin shared nodes.
- Leave the URLs unchanged. They are already world-readable, so a destination app resolves them by following the link.
- Return unusable references as part of the publish result.

### Done When

- Publishing a Roam-origin node reports how many asset references its markdown contains.
- The published markdown keeps its asset URLs unchanged.
- An unusable reference does not stop the node from publishing.

### Out of Scope

- Storing asset references in the database. No consumer reads them, and a work list can be derived from `Content.text` when one is needed.
- Copying Roam-hosted files into Supabase.
- Access scope metadata.

### Notes

- Scope reduced from the original description. See design.md, Decisions 1 and 7.
- Functional requirement F10.

---

## ENG-1872 (rewrite, then split)

**Proposed title:** Copy Obsidian-origin assets into Roam on import

**Why the rewrite:** the current description asks the importer to "consume shared asset metadata where available". No such metadata exists. The importer finds assets by parsing markdown, and the real work is an upload path plus a registry.

### Problem

- Obsidian attachments live in a private Supabase bucket. A browser cannot fetch them without credentials, and Roam embeds a file only by URL, so images in an imported node do not render.
- `roamAlphaAPI.file.upload` returns a new URL on every call, and re-sync rebuilds a page from scratch. Without a record of previous copies, every re-sync uploads every asset again.

### Solution

- Copy each referenced Obsidian asset into Roam storage during materialization.
- Record hash to URL in a graph-level asset registry, so an asset copied once is reused anywhere in the graph.
- Rewrite each asset link with Roam's embed syntax for its media type.

### Done When

- An Obsidian-origin node that references an image imports into Roam, and the image renders.
- An asset already copied into the graph is not uploaded again, whether the earlier copy came from this node or another.
- A node that references a PDF, an audio file, and an external URL produces correct Roam syntax for each.
- An asset that fails to copy keeps its original link text and appears in the import result. The node still imports.

### Out of Scope

- Deleting copied files, and tracking which copies are unused.
- Showing failures to the user. ENG-1877 covers that.
- Asset refresh after the source file changes.

### Notes

- Split into the four sub-issues below.
- See design.md, Decisions 3 to 6.

---

## Sub-issue a

**Title:** Add a graph-level asset registry accessor for Roam

### Problem

- Copying an Obsidian asset into Roam storage produces a URL that cannot be derived or predicted. Nothing can reuse a previous copy without a stored record.
- Roam offers no way to list a graph's files, so the record cannot be rebuilt by asking Roam what exists.

### Solution

- Read and write an `assetRegistry` map of content hash to URL, held in the props of a block named "Sync Asset Registry" on `[[roam/js/discourse-graph]]`.
- Create that block when it is absent.

### Done When

- A write followed by a read returns the same map.
- The accessor creates the "Sync Asset Registry" block when the page does not already contain it.
- Unit tests cover a missing block, an empty map, and a populated map.

### Out of Scope

- Copying files. Sub-issue b covers that.
- Rebuilding a registry that a user deleted.

### Notes

- Two clients in the same graph can write at once. The last write wins, and the cost is one redundant upload. Do not add locking.
- The registry is a cache, not a source of truth. Each copy is named `imported-<sha256>`, so the map can be rebuilt from the files themselves.
- Blocked by nothing. This can start immediately.

---

## Sub-issue b

**Title:** Copy one asset from Supabase into Roam storage

### Problem

- Roam embeds a file only by URL, and Obsidian assets live in a private Supabase bucket.
- The copy step needs one testable unit before materialization calls it.

### Solution

- Download the asset from the Supabase bucket, build a `File` named `imported-<sha256>.<ext>`, and pass it to `roamAlphaAPI.file.upload`.
- Extract the URL from the return value, whose shape varies by media type.
- Record the hash and URL in the asset registry after the upload succeeds.
- Skip an asset over an explicit size limit and return a skip result.

### Done When

- Copying the same hash twice performs one upload and returns the same URL.
- URL extraction handles all five return shapes: `![](url)`, `{{[[pdf]]: url}}`, `{{[[audio]]: url}}`, `{{[[video]]: url}}`, and a bare URL.
- An asset over the size limit returns a skip result instead of throwing.

### Out of Scope

- Finding assets in markdown, and rewriting links. Sub-issue c covers that.

### Notes

- Set the size limit in this ticket. Do not inherit Obsidian's publish limit, which is expected to rise.
- Record after the upload returns, not before. A placeholder written first carries no URL, so a later sync can neither reuse nor locate the upload.
- Keep the `imported-<sha256>` name. It is readable from Firebase object metadata without downloading the file, and it is the only graph-wide record of what has been copied.
- Blocked by sub-issue a.

---

## Sub-issue c

**Title:** Rewrite asset links in Obsidian-origin markdown for Roam

### Problem

- Materialized markdown carries Obsidian asset links that Roam cannot resolve.
- Roam renders each media type with its own syntax, and a bare URL renders as its own link text, which shows the reader a long storage URL instead of a filename.

### Solution

- Find asset references in the markdown and resolve each to its content hash.
- Emit Roam's embed syntax for each asset's media type.
- Label a non-media link with the source filename, so the reader sees `[report.docx](url)`.
- Leave `http` and `https` links unchanged.

### Done When

- The ENG-1864 fixtures round-trip through the rewriter.
- A node that references an image, a PDF, and an external URL produces correct Roam syntax for each.
- A non-media link shows the source filename as its link text.

### Out of Scope

- Uploading files. Sub-issue b covers that.

### Notes

- Develop against a stub that maps hash to URL, so this ticket does not wait on sub-issues a or b.
- Blocked by ENG-1864 for the fixtures.

---

## Sub-issue d

**Title:** Add an asset copy stage to Roam node materialization

### Problem

- The registry, the copy step, and the link rewriter do nothing until materialization calls them.
- An asset that fails to copy must not stop a node from importing.

### Solution

- Add a materialization stage between fetch-content and replace-page-content that copies assets and rewrites links.
- Keep the original link text for an asset that fails, and return the failure in the materialization result.

### Done When

- An Obsidian-origin node with an image imports into Roam, and the image renders.
- A node whose asset returns 404 still imports with an intact body, and the failure appears in the result.
- Re-syncing a node does not upload an asset the graph already holds.

### Out of Scope

- Showing failures to the user. ENG-1877 covers that.

### Notes

- Blocked by sub-issues b and c.

---

## ENG-1864 (no rewrite, one note to add)

Its Done When asks for typed payloads and fixtures, and the design delivers both. The deviations sit in its Solution section only. Suggested addition to Notes:

> Two items from the original solution were designed out. `accessScope` was dropped because row-level security on the referencing node already determines read access, so a per-asset field would duplicate it more weakly (Decision 7). Stored MIME type and size were dropped because no consumer reads them, and both are available from storage metadata when needed (Decision 1).

---

## ENG-1871 and ENG-1873 (no change proposed)

- ENG-1873 is close to satisfied already. Obsidian's `processLink` returns `http` and `https` links unchanged, so Roam-origin URLs survive import. The ticket may reduce to writing the test.
- ENG-1871 holds as written, though the contract it validates is smaller than the original description assumed.
